title: Black Forest Labs launches FLUX 3, a single model for image, video, audio and robot action
subtitle: The German lab's new frontier model generates 20-second audio-video clips from one prompt and extends the same architecture to robotic control, with mimic robotics already deploying it at Audi.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Black Forest Labs launched FLUX 3 on July 23, its first unified multimodal frontier model. FLUX 3 generates images, combined audio-video clips of up to 20 seconds, and — via the same backbone — action predictions for robotic control, all from a single natural-language prompt. FLUX 3 Video is available now through gated early access; image generation follows in the coming weeks; the open-weight FLUX 3 Dev backbone will land later. The action-prediction variant is rolling out through partners first, starting with mimic robotics, which has already deployed a FLUX 3-based system in tests at Audi.

The architectural bet is significant. Most frontier multimodal models — Sora, Veo, Gemini — treat video, audio and control as separate output heads sharing a text encoder. FLUX 3 trains a single network that predicts across all four modalities, including motor actions. If the approach holds up under scaling, it removes the alignment penalty of piping outputs between specialized models: the same weights that generated a video of a hand grasping a cup can, in principle, produce the joint commands to make a robot do it. That is the same theoretical claim Google DeepMind made for Gemini Robotics, and now there is a European entrant making it too.

The commercial angle is Audi. Mimic robotics, a Zurich spin-off using FLUX 3 as its action model, is running trials on Audi's production lines — the first time a European industrial customer has publicly committed to a European frontier model for physical AI. Black Forest Labs was founded by former Stability AI researchers behind Stable Diffusion, and FLUX 3 arrives as its third model family in 18 months. The gap between BFL and the U.S. video-generation leaders — Sora, Veo, Runway Gen-5 — was measured in years on release cadence a year ago; on this launch, it is measured in weeks.

For learners: the reason to pay attention to unified multimodal architectures is that they change what data you need. A single joint model can be trained on video-with-audio (abundant), but the action-prediction head needs paired video-and-motor-command data (scarce). Whoever wins the physical AI race will be whoever can assemble that paired dataset fastest, which is why every serious contender is either building robots (Tesla, Figure, Agility, mimic) or partnering with someone who does. When you read about a new 'physical AI' model, ask what data it was trained on — the answer tells you whether the release is a research demo or a real product.
